headline: New moon springs build toward a sunset striper window as fluke slide off the flats
subhead: Central Sound bass are staging for the July 11-13 high-tide dusk bite while porgies and blues fill the daylight hours.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound settled into that mid-summer holding pattern where nothing dramatic happens but everything quietly repositions. Water in the harbors — Oyster Bay, Port Jeff, the back of the Norwalk Islands — has been running warm enough that you can feel it through the hull, mid-70s in the shallow coves, while the main body of the Sound out past Stratford Shoal stays noticeably cooler underneath. That split is the whole story right now. Wind's been the typical July pattern, calm mornings, building southwest in the afternoon, nothing that's torn up the water but enough to keep bait pushed into the lees of the islands and the harbor mouths. Tides have been unremarkable the past several days — we're coming off a quarter moon, current's been moderate, nothing forcing fish to move with urgency.

That changes this week. We're building toward a new moon on the 11th-13th, and that means spring tides stacking up fast — bigger swings, stronger current, and critically, the high stand of tide starting to line up with sunset on the western end of our beat. That's the window I'm circling on the calendar. When a big incoming tide crests right as the light goes down, bass that have been sitting deep and sulky through the heat of the day get a reason to move — the current stacks bait against structure right as their most comfortable feeding light shows up. I'd be looking at the Norwalk Islands funnels, the drop at Stratford Shoal, and the mouth of Port Jeff harbor on that Friday-through-Monday high water at dusk. It's the first real evening window we've had since the full moon back in June, and if the wind lays down like it's supposed to, it should fish.

Daytime, the bass bite has been honest but not easy — scattered fish, not stacked fish. Guys working bucktails and swim shads along the Norwalk Islands rips on the last two hours of the outgoing have been picking off schoolies to maybe 28 inches, with the occasional better fish mixed in when the current really rips through the cuts. Live bunker under a balloon off Charles Island produced a few better fish last week, one report of a fish pushing 20 pounds, but that was one good afternoon out of several quiet ones — don't go out expecting that to repeat on command. The pattern that's actually consistent is first-light and last-light around structure with moving water. Middle of the day, middle of the tide, forget it — those fish are down and not interested.

Bluefish have filled in the gaps nicely and they're not shy about it. Middle Ground Light and the rips off Charles Island have both had choppers blowing up on top during the outgoing, and they'll hit anything that moves fast — Hopkins spoons, poppers, bucktails retrieved with some speed. If you want steady action rather than quality, this is where you get it right now. Bring wire or heavy fluoro leader because they're shredding light mono without hesitation.

Fluke are the interesting story this week. The bay-side water has warmed enough that the flats fish have cleared out — I'm not finding them in the shallow coves of Oyster Bay or the back bays the way we were in June. They've slid to the channels and the deeper cuts, which tracks with what's happening Sound-wide as the warm surface layer pushes bait and fluke alike toward cooler bottom structure. The Norwalk Islands channel edges in 25 to 35 feet have been the better bet, drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, working them slow along the bottom on the last of the outgoing when the current's still moving enough to keep the bait swimming naturally. Stratford Shoal's deep side has also given up a few quality fish to guys dragging squid strips tipped with Gulp. Nothing has been a slam-dunk — you're covering ground and culling through shorts to find keepers — but the fish are there if you commit to working the deeper structure instead of the shallows.

Porgies are doing exactly what porgies do in July — piling up on structure and biting steady. Charles Island rocks, the Middle Ground reef, and the rubble around Stratford Shoal have all been giving up good numbers on sandworms and clam, fished on the bottom with light tackle. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod for the kids or you just want dinner, this is your play right now, no drama required.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, are close to a non-event this season so far. Water's plenty warm enough on paper, but I haven't heard of a single solid weakfish report out of the river mouths or back bays that usually hold them this time of year. That warm-water threshold everybody points to clearly isn't the only ingredient — something else isn't lining up, whether it's bait, salinity, or just numbers being down. I wouldn't build a trip around them right now.

As for bonito — too early for us. That's an August pattern here in the Sound proper, once the water really settles and bait gets pushed hard into the funnel at the Race. The early reports coming out of the ocean side are worth watching as a leading indicator, but I wouldn't rig for them yet inside our beat.

If I had one shot this week, I'd take the Saturday or Sunday evening high around the Norwalk Islands, timed to that new-moon spring tide meeting the sunset. Bring bucktails for the bass, something fast for the blues that will inevitably show up, and don't be shy about working the deeper channel edges after dark if the bite up top goes quiet — that's where the bigger fish have been sitting all week.
